arXiv:2106.00170v3 [stat.ME] 28 Oct 2021

Adaptive Conformal Inference
Under Distribution Shift

Isaac Gibbs Affiliation: Department of Statistics Affiliation: Stanford University Email: igibbs@stanford.edu    Emmanuel J. Candès Affiliation: Department of Statistics Affiliation: Department of Mathematics Affiliation: Stanford University Email: candes@stanford.edu
Abstract

We develop methods for forming prediction sets in an online setting where the data generating distribution is allowed to vary over time in an unknown fashion. Our framework builds on ideas from conformal inference to provide a general wrapper that can be combined with any black box method that produces point predictions of the unseen label or estimated quantiles of its distribution. While previous conformal inference methods rely on the assumption that the data points are exchangeable, our adaptive approach provably achieves the desired coverage frequency over long-time intervals irrespective of the true data generating process. We accomplish this by modelling the distribution shift as a learning problem in a single parameter whose optimal value is varying over time and must be continuously re-estimated. We test our method, adaptive conformal inference, on two real world datasets and find that its predictions are robust to visible and significant distribution shifts.

1 Introduction

Machine learning algorithms are increasingly being employed in high stakes decision making processes. For instance, deep neural networks are currently being used in self-driving cars to detect nearby objects [2] and parole decisions are being made with the assistance of complex models that combine over a hundred features [1]. As the popularity of black box methods and the cost of making wrong decisions grow it is crucial that we develop tools to quantify the uncertainty of their predictions.

In this paper we develop methods for constructing prediction sets that are guaranteed to contain the target label with high probability. We focus specifically on an online learning setting in which we observe covariate-response pairs {(Xt,Yt)}t∈ℕ⊆ℝd×ℝ\{(X_{t},Y_{t})\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R} in a sequential fashion. At each time step t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N} we are tasked with using the previously observed data {(Xr,Yr)}1≤r≤t−1\{(X_{r},Y_{r})\}_{1\leq r\leq t-1} along with the new covariates, XtX_{t}, to form a prediction set C^t\hat{C}_{t} for YtY_{t}. Then, given a target coverage level α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) our generic goal is to guarantee that YtY_{t} belongs to C^t\hat{C}_{t} at least 100​(1−α)100(1-\alpha)% of the time.

Perhaps the most powerful and flexible tools for solving this problem come from conformal inference [34, 16, 32, 22, 31, 15, 3, see e.g.] . This framework provides a generic methodology for transforming the outputs of any black box prediction algorithm into a prediction set. The generality of this approach has facilitated the development of a large suite of conformal methods, each specialized to a specific prediction problem of interest [30, 11, 23, 8, 24, 21, e.g.]. With only minor exceptions all of these algorithms share the same common guarantee that if the training and test data are exchangeable, then the prediction set has valid marginal coverage ℙ⁡(Yt∈C^t)=1−α\mathbb{P}(Y_{t}\in\hat{C}_{t})=1-\alpha.

While exchangeability is a common assumption, there are many real-world applications in which we do not expect the marginal distribution of (Xt,Yt)(X_{t},Y_{t}) to be stationary. For example, in finance and economics market behaviour can shift drastically in response to new legislation or major world events. Alternatively, the distribution of (Xt,Yt)(X_{t},Y_{t}) may change as we deploy our prediction model in new environments. This paper develops adaptive conformal inference (ACI), a method for forming prediction sets that are robust to changes in the marginal distribution of the data. Our approach is both simple, in that it requires only the tracking of a single parameter that models the shift, and general as it can be combined with any modern machine learning algorithm that produces point predictions or estimated quantiles for the response. We show that over long time intervals ACI achieves the target coverage frequency without any assumptions on the data-generating distribution. Moreover, when the distribution shift is small and the prediction algorithm takes a certain simple form we show that ACI will additionally obtain approximate marginal coverage at most time steps.

1.1 Conformal inference

Suppose we are given a fitted regression model for predicting the value of YY from XX. Let yy be a candidate value for YtY_{t}. To determine if yy is a reasonable estimate of YtY_{t}, we define a conformity score S⁡(X,Y)S(X,Y) that measures how well the value yy conforms with the predictions of our fitted model. For example, if our regression model produces point predictions μ^​(X)\hat{\mu}(X) then we could use a conformity score that measures the distance between μ^​(Xt)\hat{\mu}(X_{t}) and yy. One such example is

S⁡(Xt,y)=|μ^​(Xt)−y|.S(X_{t},y)=|\hat{\mu}(X_{t})-y|.

Alternatively, suppose our regression model outputs estimates q^​(X,p)\hat{q}(X;p) of the ppth quantile of the distribution of Y|XY|X. Then, we could use the method of conformal quantile regression (CQR) [28], which examines the signed distance between yy and fitted upper and lower quantiles through the score

S⁡(Xt,y)=max⁡{q^​(Xt,α/2)−y,y−q^​(Xt,1−α/2)}.S(X_{t},y)=\max\{\hat{q}(X_{t};\alpha/2)-y,y-\hat{q}(X_{t};1-\alpha/2)\}.

Regardless of what conformity score is chosen the key issue is to determine how small S⁡(Xt,y)S(X_{t},y) should be in order to accept yy as a reasonable prediction for YtY_{t}. Assume we have a calibration set 𝒟cal⊆{(Xr,Yr)}1≤r≤t−1\mathcal{D}_{\text{cal}}\subseteq\{(X_{r},Y_{r})\}_{1\leq r\leq t-1} that is different from the data that was used to fit the regression model. Using this calibration set we define the fitted quantiles of the conformity scores to be

Q^(p):=inf{s:(1|𝒟cal|∑(Xr,Yr)∈𝒟cal𝟙{S(Xr,Yr)≤s})≥p},\hat{Q}(p):=\inf\left\{s:\left(\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\text{cal}}|}\sum_{(X_{r},Y_{r})\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{cal}}}\mathbbm{1}_{\{S(X_{r},Y_{r})\leq s\}}\right)\geq p\right\}, (1)

and say that yy is a reasonable prediction for YtY_{t} if S⁡(Xt,y)≤Q^​(1−α)S(X_{t},y)\leq\hat{Q}(1-\alpha).

The crucial observation is that if the data 𝒟cal∪{(Xt,Yt)}\mathcal{D}_{\text{cal}}\cup\{(X_{t},Y_{t})\} are exchangeable and we break ties uniformly at random then the rank of S⁡(Xt,Yt)S(X_{t},Y_{t}) amongst the points {S⁡(Xr,Yr)}(Xr,Yr)∈𝒟cal∪{S⁡(Xt,Yt)}\{S(X_{r},Y_{r})\}_{(X_{r},Y_{r})\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{cal}}}\cup\{S(X_{t},Y_{t})\} will be uniform. Therefore,

ℙ⁡(S⁡(Xt,Yt)≤Q^​(1−α))=⌈|𝒟cal|​(1−α)⌉|𝒟cal|+1.\mathbb{P}(S(X_{t},Y_{t})\leq\hat{Q}(1-\alpha))=\frac{\lceil|\mathcal{D}_{\text{cal}}|(1-\alpha)\rceil}{|\mathcal{D}_{\text{cal}}|+1}.

Thus, defining our prediction set to be C^t:={y:S⁡(Xt,y)≤Q^​(1−α)}\hat{C}_{t}:=\{y:S(X_{t},y)\leq\hat{Q}(1-\alpha)\} gives the marginal coverage guarantee

ℙ⁡(Yt∈C^t)=ℙ⁡(S⁡(Xt,Yt)≤Q^​(1−α))=⌈|𝒟cal|​(1−α)⌉|𝒟cal|+1.\mathbb{P}(Y_{t}\in\hat{C}_{t})=\mathbb{P}(S(X_{t},Y_{t})\leq\hat{Q}(1-\alpha))=\frac{\lceil|\mathcal{D}_{\text{cal}}|(1-\alpha)\rceil}{|\mathcal{D}_{\text{cal}}|+1}.

By introducing additional randomization this generic procedure can be altered slightly to produce a set C^t\hat{C}_{t} that satisfies the exact marginal coverage guarantee ℙ⁡(Yt∈C^t)=1−α\mathbb{P}(Y_{t}\in\hat{C}_{t})=1-\alpha [34]. For the purposes of this paper this adjustment is not critical and so we omit the details here. Additionally, we remark that the method outlined above is often referred to as split or inductive conformal inference [27, 34, 26]. This refers to the fact that we have split the observed data between a training set used to fit the regression model and a withheld calibration set. The adaptive conformal inference method developed in this article can also be easily adjusted to work with full conformal inference in which data splitting is avoided at the cost of greater computational resources [34].

2 Adapting conformal inference to distribution shifts

Up until this point we have been working with a single score function S⁡(⋅)S(\cdot) and quantile function Q^​(⋅)\hat{Q}(\cdot). In the general case where the distribution of the data is shifting over time both these functions should be regularly re-estimated to align with the most recent observations. Therefore, we assume that at each time tt we are given a fitted score function St​(⋅)S_{t}(\cdot) and corresponding quantile function Q^t​(⋅)\hat{Q}_{t}(\cdot). We define the realized miscoverage rate of the prediction set C^t​(α):={y:St​(Xt,y)≤Q^t​(1−α)}\hat{C}_{t}(\alpha):=\{y:S_{t}(X_{t},y)\leq\hat{Q}_{t}(1-\alpha)\} as

Mt​(α):=ℙ⁡(St​(Xt,Yt)>Q^t​(1−α)),M_{t}(\alpha):=\mathbb{P}(S_{t}(X_{t},Y_{t})>\hat{Q}_{t}(1-\alpha)),

where the probability is over the test point (Xt,Yt)(X_{t},Y_{t}) as well as the data used to fit St​(⋅)S_{t}(\cdot) and Q^t​(⋅)\hat{Q}_{t}(\cdot).

Now, since the distribution generating the data is non-stationary we do not expect Mt​(α)M_{t}(\alpha) to be equal, or even close to, α\alpha. Even so, we can still postulate that if the conformity scores used to fit Q^t​(⋅)\hat{Q}_{t}(\cdot) cover the bulk of the distribution of St​(Xt,Yt)S_{t}(X_{t},Y_{t}) then there may be an alternative value αt∗∈[0,1]\alpha^{*}_{t}\in[0,1] such that Mt​(αt∗)≅αM_{t}(\alpha^{*}_{t})\cong\alpha. More rigorously, assume that with probability one, Q^t​(⋅)\hat{Q}_{t}(\cdot) is continuous, non-decreasing and such that Q^t​(0)=−∞\hat{Q}_{t}(0)=-\infty and Q^t​(1)=∞\hat{Q}_{t}(1)=\infty. This does not hold for the split conformal quantile functions defined in (1), but in the case where there are no ties amongst the conformity scores we can adjust our definition to guarantee this by smoothing over the jump discontinuities in Q^​(⋅)\hat{Q}(\cdot). Then, Mt​(⋅)M_{t}(\cdot) will be non-decreasing on [0,1][0,1] with Mt​(0)=0M_{t}(0)=0 and Mt​(1)=1M_{t}(1)=1 and so we may define

αt∗:=sup{β∈[0,1]:Mt​(β)≤α}.\alpha^{*}_{t}:=\sup\{\beta\in[0,1]:M_{t}(\beta)\leq\alpha\}.

Moreover, if we additionally assume that

ℙ⁡(St​(Xt,Yt)=Q^t​(1−αt∗))=0,\mathbb{P}(S_{t}(X_{t},Y_{t})=\hat{Q}_{t}(1-\alpha^{*}_{t}))=0,

then we will have that Mt​(αt∗)=αM_{t}(\alpha^{*}_{t})=\alpha. So, in particular we find that by correctly calibrating the argument to Q^t​(⋅)\hat{Q}_{t}(\cdot) we can achieve either approximate or exact marginal coverage.

To perform this calibration we will use a simple online update. This update proceeds by examining the empirical miscoverage frequency of the previous prediction sets and then decreasing (resp. increasing) our estimate of αt∗\alpha^{*}_{t} if the prediction sets were historically under-covering (resp. over-covering) YtY_{t}. In particular, let α1\alpha_{1} denote our initial estimate (in our experiments we will choose α1=α\alpha_{1}=\alpha). Recursively define the sequence of miscoverage events

errt:={1, if ​Yt∉C^t​(αt),0​, otherwise,​ where ​C^t​(αt):={y:St​(Xt,y)≤Q^t​(1−αt)}.\text{err}_{t}:=\begin{cases}1,\text{ if }Y_{t}\notin\hat{C}_{t}(\alpha_{t}),\\ 0\text{, otherwise,}\end{cases}\text{ where }\hat{C}_{t}(\alpha_{t}):=\{y:S_{t}(X_{t},y)\leq\hat{Q}_{t}(1-\alpha_{t})\}.

Then, fixing a step size parameter γ>0\gamma>0 we consider the simple online update

αt+1:=αt+γ⁡(α−errt).\alpha_{t+1}:=\alpha_{t}+\gamma(\alpha-\text{err}_{t}). (2)

We refer to this algorithm as adaptive conformal inference. Here, errt\text{err}_{t} plays the role of our estimate of the historical miscoverage frequency. A natural alternative to this is the update

αt+1=αt+γ⁡(α−∑s=1tws​errs),\alpha_{t+1}=\alpha_{t}+\gamma\left(\alpha-\sum_{s=1}^{t}w_{s}\text{err}_{s}\right), (3)

where {ws}1≤s≤t⊆[0,1]\{w_{s}\}_{1\leq s\leq t}\subseteq[0,1] is a sequence of increasing weights with ∑s=1tws=1\sum_{s=1}^{t}w_{s}=1. This update has the appeal of more directly evaluating the recent empirical miscoverage frequency when deciding whether or not to lower or raise αt\alpha_{t}. In practice, we find that (2) and (3) produce almost identical results. For example, in Section A.3 in the Appendix we show some sample trajectories for αt\alpha_{t} obtained using the update (3) with

ws:=0.95t−s∑s′=1t0.95t−s′.w_{s}:=\frac{0.95^{t-s}}{\sum_{s^{\prime}=1}^{t}0.95^{t-s^{\prime}}}.

We find that these trajectories are very similar to those produced by (2). The main difference is that the trajectories obtained with (3) are smoother with less local variation in αt\alpha_{t}. In the remainder of this article we will focus on (2) for simplicity.

2.1 Choosing the step size

The choice of γ\gamma gives a tradeoff between adaptability and stability. While raising the value of γ\gamma will make the method more adaptive to observed distribution shifts, it will also induce greater volatility in the value of αt\alpha_{t}. In practice, large fluctuations in αt\alpha_{t} may be undesirable as it allows the method to oscillate between outputting small conservative and large anti-conservative prediction sets.

In Theorem 4.2 we give an upper bound on (Mt​(αt)−α)2(M_{t}(\alpha_{t})-\alpha)^{2} that is optimized by choosing γ\gamma proportional to |αt+1∗−αt∗|\sqrt{|\alpha^{*}_{t+1}-\alpha^{*}_{t}|}. While not directly applicable in practice, this result supports the intuition that in environments with greater distributional shift the algorithm needs to be more adapatable and thus γ\gamma should be chosen to be larger. In our experiments we will take γ=0.005\gamma=0.005. This value was chosen because it was found to give relatively stable trajectories for αt\alpha_{t} while still being sufficiently large as to allow αt\alpha_{t} to adapt to observed shifts. In agreement with the general principles outlined above we found that larger values of γ\gamma also successfully protect against distribution shifts, while taking γ\gamma to be too small causes adaptive conformal inference to perform similar to non-adaptive methods that hold αt=α\alpha_{t}=\alpha constant across time.

2.2 Real data example: predicting market volatility

We apply ACI to the prediction of market volatility. Let {Pt}1≤t≤T\{P_{t}\}_{1\leq t\leq T} denote a sequence of daily open prices for a stock. For all t≥2t\geq 2, define the return Rt:=(Pt−Pt−1)/Pt−1R_{t}:=(P_{t}-P_{t-1})/P_{t-1} and realized volatility Vt=Rt2V_{t}=R_{t}^{2}. Our goal is to use the previously observed returns Xt:={Rs}1≤s≤t−1X_{t}:=\{R_{s}\}_{1\leq s\leq t-1} to form prediction sets for Yt:=VtY_{t}:=V_{t}. More sophisticated financial models might augment XtX_{t} with additional market covariates (available to the analyst at time t−1t-1). As the primary purpose of this section is to illustrate adaptive conformal inference we work with only a simple prediction method.

We start off by forming point predictions using a GARCH(1,1) model [4]. This method assumes that Rt=σt​ϵtR_{t}=\sigma_{t}\epsilon_{t} with ϵ2,…,ϵT\epsilon_{2},\dots,\epsilon_{T} taken to be i.i.d. 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1) and σt\sigma_{t} satisfying the recursive update

σt2=ω+τ​Vt−1+β​σt−12.\sigma_{t}^{2}=\omega+\tau V_{t-1}+\beta\sigma_{t-1}^{2}.

This is a common approach used for forecasting volatility in economics. In practice, shifting market dynamics can cause the predictions of this model to become inaccurate over large time periods. Thus, when forming point predictions we fit the model using only the last 1250 trading days (i.e. approximately 5 years) of market data. More precisely, for all times t>1250t>1250 we fit the coefficients ω^t,τ^t,β^t\hat{\omega}_{t},\ \hat{\tau}_{t},\hat{\beta}_{t} as well as the sequence of variances {σ^st}1≤s≤t−1\{\hat{\sigma}^{t}_{s}\}_{1\leq s\leq t-1} using only the data {Rr}t−1250≤r<t\{R_{r}\}_{t-1250\leq r<t}. Then, our point prediction for the realized volatility at time tt is

(σ^tt)2:=ω^t+τ^t​Vt−1+β^t​(σ^t−1t)2.(\hat{\sigma}^{t}_{t})^{2}:=\hat{\omega}_{t}+\hat{\tau}_{t}V_{t-1}+\hat{\beta}_{t}(\hat{\sigma}^{t}_{t-1})^{2}.

To form prediction intervals we define the sequence of conformity scores

St:=|Vt−(σ^tt)2|(σ^tt)2S_{t}:=\frac{|V_{t}-(\hat{\sigma}^{t}_{t})^{2}|}{(\hat{\sigma}^{t}_{t})^{2}}

and the corresponding quantile function

Q^t​(p):=inf{x:11250​∑r=t−1250t−1𝟙Sr≤x≥p}.\hat{Q}_{t}(p):=\inf\left\{x:\frac{1}{1250}\sum_{r=t-1250}^{t-1}\mathbbm{1}_{S_{r}\leq x}\geq p\right\}.

Then, our prediction set at time tt is

C^t​(αt):={v:|v−(σ^tt)2|(σ^tt)2≤Q^t​(1−αt)},\hat{C}_{t}(\alpha_{t}):=\left\{v:\frac{|v-(\hat{\sigma}^{t}_{t})^{2}|}{(\hat{\sigma}^{t}_{t})^{2}}\leq\hat{Q}_{t}(1-\alpha_{t})\right\},

where {αt}\{\alpha_{t}\} is initialized with α1250=α=0.1\alpha_{1250}=\alpha=0.1 and then updated recursively as in (2).

We compare this algorithm to a non-adaptive alternative that takes αt=α\alpha_{t}=\alpha fixed. To measure the performance of these methods across time we examine their local coverage frequencies defined as the average coverage rate over the most recent two years, i.e.

localCovt:=1−1500​∑r=t−250+1t+250errr.\text{localCov}_{t}:=1-\frac{1}{500}\sum_{r=t-250+1}^{t+250}\text{err}_{r}. (4)

If the methods perform well then we expect the local coverage frequency to stay near the target value 1−α1-\alpha across all time points.

Daily open prices were obtained from publicly available datasets published by The Wall Street Journal. The realized local coverage frequencies for the non-adaptive and adaptive conformal methods on four different stocks are shown in Figure 1. These stocks were selected out of a total of 12 stocks that we examined because they showed a clear failure of the non-adaptive method. Adaptive conformal inference was found to perform well in all cases (see Figure 9 in the appendix).

As a visual comparator, the grey curves show the moving average 1−1500​∑r=t−250+1t+250Ir1-\frac{1}{500}\sum_{r=t-250+1}^{t+250}I_{r} for sequences {It}1≤t≤T\{I_{t}\}_{1\leq t\leq T} that are i.i.d. Bernoulli(0.1). We see that the local coverage frequencies obtained by adaptive conformal inference (blue lines) always stay within the variation that would be expected from an i.i.d. Bernoulli sequence. On the other hand, the non-adaptive method undergoes large excursions away from the target level of 1−α=0.91-\alpha=0.9 (red lines). For example, in the bottom right panel we can see that the non-adaptive method fails to cover the realized volatility of Fannie Mae during the 2008 financial crisis, while the adaptive method is robust to this event (see Figure 4 in the Appendix for a plot of the price of Fannie Mae over this time period).

3 Related Work

Prior work on conformal inference has considered two different types of distribution shift [33, 10]. In both cases the focus was on environments in which the calibration data is drawn i.i.d. from a single distribution P0P_{0}, while the test point comes from a second distribution P1P_{1}. In this setting Tibshirani et al. [33] showed that valid prediction sets can be obtained by re-weighting the calibration data using the likelihood ratio between P1P_{1} and P0P_{0}. However, this requires the conditional distribution of Y|XY|X to be constant between training and testing and the likelihood ratio P1​(X)/P0​(X)P_{1}(X)/P_{0}(X) to be either known or very accurately estimated. On the other hand, Cauchois et al. [10] develop methods for forming prediction sets that are valid whenever P1P_{1} and P0P_{0} are close in ff-divergence. Similar to our work, they show that if Df(P1||P0)≤ρD_{f}(P_{1}||P_{0})\leq\rho then there exists a conservative value αρ∈(0,1)\alpha_{\rho}\in(0,1) such that

M⁡(αρ):=ℙ⁡(S⁡(Xt,Yt)>Q^​(1−αρ))≤α.M(\alpha_{\rho}):=\mathbb{P}(S(X_{t},Y_{t})>\hat{Q}(1-\alpha_{\rho}))\leq\alpha.

The difference between our approach and theirs is twofold. First, while they fix a single conservative value αρ\alpha_{\rho} our methods aim to estimate the optimal choice α∗\alpha^{*} satisfying M⁡(α∗)=αM(\alpha^{*})=\alpha. This is not possible in the setting of [10] as they do not observe any data from which the size of the distribution shift can be estimated. Second, while they consider only one training and one testing distribution we work in a fully online setting in which the distribution is allowed to shift continuously over time.

4 Coverage guarantees

4.1 Distribution-free results

In this section we outline the theoretical coverage guarantees of adaptive conformal inference. We will assume throughout that with probability one α1∈[0,1]\alpha_{1}\in[0,1] and Q^t\hat{Q}_{t} is non-decreasing with Q^t​(x)=−∞\hat{Q}_{t}(x)=-\infty for all x<0x<0 and Q^t​(x)=∞\hat{Q}_{t}(x)=\infty for all x>1x>1. Our first result shows that over long time intervals adaptive conformal inference obtains the correct coverage frequency irrespective of any assumptions on the data-generating distribution.

Lemma 4.1

With probability one we have that ∀t∈ℕ\forall t\in\mathbb{N}, αt∈[−γ,1+γ]\alpha_{t}\in[-\gamma,1+\gamma].

Proof:

Assume by contradiction that with positive probability {αt}t∈ℕ\{\alpha_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}} is such that inftαt<−γ\inf_{t}\alpha_{t}<-\gamma (the case where suptαt>1+γ\sup_{t}\alpha_{t}>1+\gamma is identical). Note that supt|αt+1−αt|=suptγ​|α−errt|<γ\sup_{t}|\alpha_{t+1}-\alpha_{t}|=\sup_{t}\gamma|\alpha-\text{err}_{t}|<\gamma. Thus, with positive probability we may find t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N} such that αt<0\alpha_{t}<0 and αt+1<αt\alpha_{t+1}<\alpha_{t}. However,

αt<0⟹Q^t​(1−αt)=∞⟹errt=0⟹αt+1=αt+γ⁡(α−errt)≥αt\alpha_{t}<0\implies\hat{Q}_{t}(1-\alpha_{t})=\infty\implies\text{err}_{t}=0\implies\alpha_{t+1}=\alpha_{t}+\gamma(\alpha-\text{err}_{t})\geq\alpha_{t}

and thus ℙ⁡(∃t​ such that ​αt+1<αt<0)=0\mathbb{P}(\exists t\text{ such that }\alpha_{t+1}<\alpha_{t}<0)=0. We have reached a contradiction. □\square

Proposition 4.1

With probability one we have that for all T∈ℕT\in\mathbb{N},

|1T​∑t=1Terrt−α|≤max⁡{α1,1−α1}+γT​γ.\left|\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\text{err}_{t}-\alpha\right|\leq\frac{\max\{\alpha_{1},1-\alpha_{1}\}+\gamma}{T\gamma}. (5)

In particular, limT→∞1T​∑t=1Terrt=a.s.α.\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\text{err}_{t}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle a.s.}}{{=}}\alpha.

Proof:

By expanding the recursion defined in (2) and applying Lemma 4.1 we find that

[−γ,1+γ]∋αT+1=α1+∑t=1Tγ⁡(α−errt).[-\gamma,1+\gamma]\ni\alpha_{T+1}=\alpha_{1}+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma(\alpha-\text{err}_{t}).

Rearranging this gives the result. □\square

Proposition 4.1 puts no constraints on the data generating distribution. One may immediately ask whether these results can be improved by making mild assumptions on the distribution shifts. We argue that without assumptions on the quality of the initialization the answer to this question is negative. To understand this, consider a setting in which there is a single fixed optimal target α∗∈[0,1]\alpha^{*}\in[0,1] and assume that

Mt​(p)=M⁡(p)={α+1−α1−α∗​(p−α∗), if ​p>α∗,α+αα∗​(p−α∗)​ if ​p≤α∗..M_{t}(p)=M(p)=\begin{cases}\alpha+\frac{1-\alpha}{1-\alpha^{*}}(p-\alpha^{*}),\text{ if }p>\alpha^{*},\\ \alpha+\frac{\alpha}{\alpha^{*}}(p-\alpha^{*})\text{ if }p\leq\alpha^{*}.\end{cases}.

Suppose additionally that 𝔼⁡[errt|αt]=M⁡(αt)\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{t}|\alpha_{t}]=M(\alpha_{t}).11 1 This last assumption is in general only true if Q^t​(⋅)\hat{Q}_{t}(\cdot) and αt\alpha_{t} are fit independently of one another. In order to simplify the calculations consider the noiseless update αt+1=αt+γ⁡(α−M⁡(αt))=αt+γ⁡(α−𝔼⁡[errt|αt])\alpha_{t+1}=\alpha_{t}+\gamma(\alpha-M(\alpha_{t}))=\alpha_{t}+\gamma(\alpha-\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{t}|\alpha_{t}]). Intuitively, the noiseless update can be viewed as the average case behaviour of (2). Now, for any initialization α1\alpha_{1} and any γ≤min⁡{1−α∗1−α,α∗α}\gamma\leq\min\{\frac{1-\alpha^{*}}{1-\alpha},\frac{\alpha^{*}}{\alpha}\} there exists a constant c∈{1−α1−α∗,αα∗}c\in\{\frac{1-\alpha}{1-\alpha^{*}},\frac{\alpha}{\alpha^{*}}\} such that for all tt, M⁡(αt)−α=c⁡(αt−α∗)M(\alpha_{t})-\alpha=c(\alpha_{t}-\alpha^{*}). So, we have that

𝔼⁡[errt]−α=c​𝔼​[αt−α∗]=c​𝔼​[αt−1+γ⁡(α−Mt−1​(αt−1))−α∗]=c⁡(1−c​γ)​𝔼​[αt−1−α∗].\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{t}]-\alpha=c\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{t}-\alpha^{*}]=c\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{t-1}+\gamma(\alpha-M_{t-1}(\alpha_{t-1}))-\alpha^{*}]=c(1-c\gamma)\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{t-1}-\alpha^{*}].

Repeating this calculation recursively gives that

𝔼⁡[errt]−α=c​(1−c​γ)t−1​𝔼​[α1−α∗]=c​(1−c​γ)t−1​(α1−α∗),\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{t}]-\alpha=c(1-c\gamma)^{t-1}\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{1}-\alpha^{*}]=c(1-c\gamma)^{t-1}(\alpha_{1}-\alpha^{*}),

and thus,

|1T​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[errt]−α|=1−(1−c​γ)TT​γ​|α1−α∗|.\left|\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{t}]-\alpha\right|=\frac{1-(1-c\gamma)^{T}}{T\gamma}|\alpha_{1}-\alpha^{*}|.

The comparison of this bound to (5) is self-evident. The main difference is that we have replaced max⁡{1−α1,α1}\max\{1-\alpha_{1},\alpha_{1}\} with |α1−α∗||\alpha_{1}-\alpha^{*}|. This arises from the fact that α∗∈(0,1)\alpha^{*}\in(0,1) is arbitrary and thus max⁡{1−α1,α1}\max\{1-\alpha_{1},\alpha_{1}\} is the best possible upper bound on |α1−α∗||\alpha_{1}-\alpha^{*}|. So, we view Proposition 4.1 as both an agnostic guarantee that shows that our method gives the correct long-term empirical coverage frequency irrespective of the true data generating process, and as an approximately tight bound on the worst-case behaviour immediately after initialization.

4.2 Performance in a hidden Markov model

Although we believe Proposition 4.1 is an approximately tight characterization of the behaviour after initialization, we can still ask whether better bounds can be obtained for large time steps. In this section we answer this question positively by showing that if α1\alpha_{1} is initialized appropriately and the distribution shift is small, then tighter coverage guarantees can be given. In order to obtain useful results we will make some simplifying assumptions about the data generating process. While we do not expect these assumptions to hold exactly in any real-world setting, we do consider our results to be representative of the true behaviour of adaptive conformal inference and we expect similar results to hold under alternative models.

4.2.1 Setting

We model the data as coming from a hidden Markov model. In particular, we let {At}t∈ℕ⊆𝒜\{A_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\mathcal{A} denote the underlying Markov chain for the environment and we assume that conditional on {At}t∈ℕ\{A_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}}, {(Xt,Yt)}t∈ℕ\{(X_{t},Y_{t})\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}} is an independent sequence with (Xt,Yt)∼PAt(X_{t},Y_{t})\sim P_{A_{t}} for some collection of distributions {Pa:a∈𝒜}\{P_{a}:a\in\mathcal{A}\}. In order to simplify our calculations, we assume additionally that the estimated quantile function Q^t​(⋅)\hat{Q}_{t}(\cdot) and score function St​(⋅)S_{t}(\cdot) do not depend on tt and we denote them by Q^​(⋅)\hat{Q}(\cdot) and S⁡(⋅)S(\cdot). This occurs for example in the split conformal setting with fixed training and calibration sets.

In this setting, {(αt,At)}t∈ℕ\{(\alpha_{t},A_{t})\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}} forms a Markov chain on [−γ,1+γ]×𝒜[-\gamma,1+\gamma]\times\mathcal{A}. We assume that this chain has a unique stationary distribution π\pi and that (α1,A1)∼π(\alpha_{1},A_{1})\sim\pi. This implies that (αt,At,errt)(\alpha_{t},A_{t},\text{err}_{t}) is a stationary process and thus will greatly simplify our characterization of the behaviour of errt\text{err}_{t}. While there is little doubt that the theory can be extended, recall our that main goal is to get useful and simple results. That said, what we really have in mind here is that {At}t∈ℕ\{A_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}} is sufficiently well-behaved to guarantee that (αt,At)(\alpha_{t},A_{t}) has a limiting stationary distribution. In Section A.5 we give an example where this is indeed provably the case. Lastly, the assumption that (α1,A1)∼π(\alpha_{1},A_{1})\sim\pi is essentially equivalent to assuming that we have been running the algorithm for long enough to exit the initialization phase described in Section 4.1.

4.2.2 Large deviation bound for the errors

Our first observation is that errt\text{err}_{t} has the correct average value. More precisely, by Proposition 4.1 we have that limT→∞T−1​∑t=1Terrt=a.s.α\lim_{T\to\infty}T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\text{err}_{t}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle a.s.}}{{=}}\alpha and since errt\text{err}_{t} is stationary it follows that 𝔼⁡[errt]=α\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{t}]=\alpha. Thus, to understand the deviation of T−1​∑t=1TerrtT^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\text{err}_{t} from α\alpha we simply need to characterize the dependence structure of {errt}t∈ℕ\{\text{err}_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}}.

We accomplish this in Theorem 4.1, which gives a large deviation bound on |T−1​∑t=1Terrt−α||T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\text{err}_{t}-\alpha|. The idea behind this result is to decompose the dependence in {errt}t∈ℕ\{\text{err}_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}} into two parts. First, there is dependence due to the fact that αt\alpha_{t} is a function of {errr}1≤r≤t−1\{\text{err}_{r}\}_{1\leq r\leq t-1}. In Section A.7 in the Appendix we argue that this dependence induces a negative correlation and thus the errors concentrate around their expectation at a rate no slower than that of an i.i.d. Bernoulli sequence. This gives rise to the first term in (6), which is what would be obtained by applying Hoeffding’s inequality to an i.i.d. sequence. Second, there is dependence due to the fact that AtA_{t} depends on At−1A_{t-1}. More specifically, consider a setting in which the distribution of Y|XY|X has more variability in some states than others. The goal of adaptive conformal inference is to adapt to the level of variability and thus return larger prediction sets in states where the distribution of Y|XY|X is more spread. However, this algorithm is not perfect and as a result there may be some states a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A} in which 𝔼⁡[errt|At=a]\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{t}|A_{t}=a] is biased away from α\alpha. Furthermore, if the environment tends to spend long stretches of time in more variable (or less variable) states this will induce a positive dependence in the errors and cause T−1​∑t=1TerrtT^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\text{err}_{t} to deviate from α\alpha. To control this dependence we use a Bernstein inequality for Markov chains to bound |T−1​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[errt|At]−α||T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{t}|A_{t}]-\alpha|. This gives rise to the second term in (6).

Theorem 4.1

Assume that {At}t∈ℕ\{A_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}} has non-zero absolute spectral gap 1−η>01-\eta>0. Let

B:=supa∈𝒜|𝔼⁡[errt|At=a]−α| and σB2:=𝔼⁡[(𝔼⁡[errt|At]−α)2].B:=\sup_{a\in\mathcal{A}}|\mathbb{E}[\textup{err}_{t}|A_{t}=a]-\alpha|\ \ \ \text{ and }\ \ \ \sigma^{2}_{B}:=\mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{E}[\textup{err}_{t}|A_{t}]-\alpha)^{2}].

Then,

ℙ⁡(|1T​∑t=1Terrt−α|≥ϵ)≤2​exp⁡(−T​ϵ28)+2​exp⁡(−T⁡(1−η)​ϵ28​(1+η)​σB2+20​B​ϵ).\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\textup{err}_{t}-\alpha\right|\geq\epsilon\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{T\epsilon^{2}}{8}\right)+2\exp\left(-\frac{T(1-\eta)\epsilon^{2}}{8(1+\eta)\sigma^{2}_{B}+20B\epsilon}\right). (6)

A formal proof of this result can be found in Section A.7. The quality of this concentration inequality will depend critically on the size of the bias terms BB and σB2\sigma^{2}_{B}. Before proceeding, it is important that we emphasize that the definitions of BB and σB2\sigma^{2}_{B} are independent of the choice of tt owing to the fact that (αt,At,errt)(\alpha_{t},A_{t},\text{err}_{t}) is assumed stationary. Now, to understand these quantities, let

M⁡(p|a):=ℙ⁡(S⁡(Xt,Yt)>Q^​(1−p)|At=a)M(p|a):=\mathbb{P}(S(X_{t},Y_{t})>\hat{Q}(1-p)|A_{t}=a)

denote the realized miscoverage level in state a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A} obtained by the quantile Q^​(1−p)\hat{Q}(1-p). Assume that M⁡(p|a)M(p|a) is continuous. This will happen for example when Q^​(⋅)\hat{Q}(\cdot) is continuous and S⁡(Xt,Yt)|At=aS(X_{t},Y_{t})|A_{t}=a is continuously distributed. Then, there exists an optimal value αa∗\alpha^{*}_{a} such that M⁡(αa∗|a)=αM(\alpha^{*}_{a}|a)=\alpha. Lemma A.4 in the Appendix shows that if in addition M(⋅|a)M(\cdot|a) admits a second order Taylor expansion, then

B≤C⁡(γ+γ−1​supa∈𝒜supk∈ℕ𝔼⁡[|αAt+1∗−αAt∗||At+k=a]) and σB2≤B2.B\leq C\left(\gamma+\gamma^{-1}\sup_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\sup_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbb{E}[|\alpha^{*}_{A_{t+1}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}}|\big|A_{t+k}=a]\right)\ \ \ \text{ and }\ \ \ \sigma^{2}_{B}\leq B^{2}.

Here, the constant CC will depend on how much M(⋅|a)M(\cdot|a) differs from the ideal case in which Q^​(⋅)\hat{Q}(\cdot) is the true quantile function for S⁡(Xt,Yt)|At=aS(X_{t},Y_{t})|A_{t}=a. In this case we would have that M(⋅|a)M(\cdot|a) is the linear function M⁡(p|a)=pM(p|a)=p, ∀p∈[0,1]\forall p\in[0,1] and C≤2C\leq 2.

We remark that the term 𝔼⁡[|αAt+1∗−αAt∗||At+k=a]\mathbb{E}[|\alpha^{*}_{A_{t+1}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}}|\big|A_{t+k}=a] can be seen as a quantitative measurement of the size of the distribution shift in terms of the change in the critical value αa∗\alpha^{*}_{a}. Thus, we interpret these results as showing that if the distribution shift is small and ∀a∈𝒜\forall a\in\mathcal{A}, Q^​(⋅)\hat{Q}(\cdot) gives reasonable coverage of the distribution of S⁡(Xt,Yt)|At=aS(X_{t},Y_{t})|A_{t}=a, then T−1​∑t=1TerrtT^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\text{err}_{t} will concentrate well around α\alpha.

4.2.3 Achieving approximate marginal coverage

Theorem 4.1 bounds the distance between the average miscoverage rate and the target level over long stretches of time. On the other hand, it provides no information about the marginal coverage frequency at a single time step. The following result shows that if the distribution shift is small, the realized marginal coverage rate M⁡(αt|At)M(\alpha_{t}|A_{t}) will be close to α\alpha on average.

Theorem 4.2

Assume that there exists a constant L>0L>0 such that for all a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A} and all α1,α2∈ℝ\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\in\mathbb{R},

|M⁡(α2|a)−M⁡(α1|a)|≤L​|α2−α1|.|M(\alpha_{2}|a)-M(\alpha_{1}|a)|\leq L|\alpha_{2}-\alpha_{1}|.

Assume additionally that for all a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A} there exists αa∗∈(0,1)\alpha^{*}_{a}\in(0,1) such that M⁡(αa∗|a)=αM(\alpha^{*}_{a}|a)=\alpha. Then,

𝔼⁡[(M⁡(αt|At)−α)2]≤L⁡(1+γ)γ​𝔼​[|αAt+1∗−αAt∗|]+L2​γ.\mathbb{E}[(M(\alpha_{t}|A_{t})-\alpha)^{2}]\leq\frac{L(1+\gamma)}{\gamma}\mathbb{E}[|\alpha^{*}_{A_{t+1}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}}|]+\frac{L}{2}\gamma. (7)

Once again we emphasize that (7) holds for any choice of tt owing to the fact that (αt,At,errt)(\alpha_{t},A_{t},\text{err}_{t}) is assumed stationary and thus the quantities appearing in the bound are invariant across tt. Proof of this result can be found in Section A.8 of the Appendix. We remark that the right-hand side of (7) is minimized by choosing γ=(2​𝔼​[|αAt+1∗−αAt∗|])1/2\gamma=(2\mathbb{E}[|\alpha^{*}_{A_{t+1}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}}|])^{1/2}, which gives the inequality

𝔼⁡[(M⁡(αt|At)−α)2]≤L⁡(2+1)​𝔼⁡[|αAt+1∗−αAt∗|].\mathbb{E}[(M(\alpha_{t}|A_{t})-\alpha)^{2}]\leq L(\sqrt{2}+1)\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[|\alpha^{*}_{A_{t+1}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}}|]}.

As above we have that in the ideal case Q^​(⋅)\hat{Q}(\cdot) is a perfect estimate of the quantiles of S⁡(Xt,Yt)|At=aS(X_{t},Y_{t})|A_{t}=a and thus M⁡(p|a)=pM(p|a)=p and L=1L=1. Moreover, we once again have the interpretation that 𝔼⁡[|αAt+1∗−αAt∗|]\mathbb{E}[|\alpha^{*}_{A_{t+1}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}}|] is a quantitative measurement of the distribution shift. Thus, this result can be interpreted as bounding the average difference between the realized and target marginal coverage in terms of the size of the underlying distribution shift. Finally, note that the choice γ=(2​𝔼​[|αAt+1∗−αAt∗|])1/2\gamma=(2\mathbb{E}[|\alpha^{*}_{A_{t+1}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}}|])^{1/2} formalizes our intuition that γ\gamma should be chosen to be larger in domains with greater distribution shift, while not being so large as to cause αt\alpha_{t} to be overly volatile.

5 Impact of 𝑺𝒕​(⋅)\boldsymbol{S_{t}}(\cdot) on the performance

The performance of all conformal inference methods depends heavily on the design of the conformity score. Previous work has shown how carefully chosen scores or even explicit optimization of the interval width can be used to obtain smaller prediction sets [28, 29, 20, 12, e.g.]. Adaptive conformal inference can work with any conformity score St​(⋅)S_{t}(\cdot) and quantile function Q^t​(⋅)\hat{Q}_{t}(\cdot) and thus can be directly combined with other improvements in conformal inference to obtain shorter intervals. One important caveat here is that the lengths of conformal prediction sets depend directly on the quality of the fitted regression model. Thus, to obtain smaller intervals one should re-fit the model at each time step using the most recent data to build the most accurate predictions. This is exactly what we have done in our experiments in Sections 2.2 and 6.

In addition to this, the choice of St​(⋅)S_{t}(\cdot) can also have a direct effect on the coverage properties of adaptive conformal inference. Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 show that the performance of adaptive conformal inference is controlled by the size of the shift in the optimal parameter αt∗\alpha^{*}_{t} across time. Moreover, αt∗\alpha^{*}_{t} itself is in one-to-one correspondence with the 1−α1-\alpha quantile of St​(Xt,Yt)S_{t}(X_{t},Y_{t}). Thus, the coverage properties of adaptive conformal inference depend on how close St​(Xt,Yt)S_{t}(X_{t},Y_{t}) is to being stationary.

For a simple example illustrating the impact of this dependence, note that in Section 2.2 we formed prediction sets using the conformity score

St:=|Vt−σ^t2|σ^t2.S_{t}:=\frac{|V_{t}-\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{t}|}{\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{t}}.

An a priori reasonable alternative to this is the unnormalized score

S~t:=|Vt−σ^t2|.\tilde{S}_{t}:=|V_{t}-\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{t}|.

However, after a more careful examination it becomes unsurprising that normalization by σ^t2\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{t} is critical for obtaining an approximately stationary conformity score and thus S~t\tilde{S}_{t} leads to much worse coverage properties. Figure 2 shows the local coverage frequency (see (4)) of adaptive conformal inference using S~t\tilde{S}_{t}. In comparison to Figure 1 the coverage now undergoes much wider swings away from the target level of 0.9. This issue can be partially mitigated by choosing a larger value of γ\gamma that gives greater adaptivity to the algorithm.

6 Real data example: election night predictions

During the 2020 US presidential election The Washington Post used conformalized quantile regression (CQR) (see (1) and Section 1.1) to produce county level predictions of the vote total on election night [13]. Here we replicate the core elements of this method using both fixed and adaptive quantiles.

To make the setting precise, let {Yt}1≤t≤T\{Y_{t}\}_{1\leq t\leq T} denote the number of votes cast for presidential candidate Joe Biden in the 2020 election in each of approximately T=3000T=3000 counties in the United States. Let XtX_{t} denote a set of demographic covariates associated to the ttth county. In our experiment XtX_{t} will include information on the make-up of the county population by ethnicity, age, sex, median income and education (see Section A.6.1 for details). On election night county vote totals were observed as soon as the vote count was completed. If the order in which vote counts completed was uniformly random {(Xt,Yt)}1≤t≤T\{(X_{t},Y_{t})\}_{1\leq t\leq T} would be an exchangeable sequence on which we could run standard conformal inference methods. In reality, larger urban counties tend to report results later than smaller rural counties and counties on the east coast of the US report earlier than those on the west coast. Thus, the distribution of (Xt,Yt)(X_{t},Y_{t}) can be viewed as drifting throughout election night.

We apply CQR to predict the county-level vote totals (see Section A.6.2 for details). To replicate the east to west coast bias observed on election night we order the counties by their time zone with eastern time counties appearing first and Hawaiian counties appearing last. Within each time zone counties are ordered uniformly at random. Figure 3 shows the realized local coverage frequency over the most recent 300 counties (see (4)) for the non-adaptive and adaptive conformal methods. We find that the non-adaptive method fails to maintain the desired 90%90\% coverage level, incurring large troughs in its coverage frequency during time zone changes. On the other hand, the adaptive method maintains approximate 90%90\% coverage across all time points with deviations in its local coverage level comparable to what is observed in Bernoulli sequences.

7 Discussion

There are still many open problems in this area. The methods we develop are specific to cases where YtY_{t} is revealed at each time point. However, there are many settings in which we receive the response in a delayed fashion or in large batches. In addition, our theoretical results in Section 4.2 are limited to a single model for the data generating distribution and the special case where the quantile function Q^t​(⋅)\hat{Q}_{t}(\cdot) is fixed across time. It would be interesting to determine if similar results can be obtained in settings where Q^t​(⋅)\hat{Q}_{t}(\cdot) is fit in an online fashion on the most recent data. Another potential area for improvement is in the choice of the step size γ\gamma. In Section 2.1 we give some heuristic guidelines for choosing γ\gamma based on the size of the distribution shift in the environment. Ideally however we would like to be able to determine γ\gamma adaptively without prior knowledge. Finally, our experimental results are limited to just two domains. Additional work is needed to determine if our methods can successfully protect against a wider variety of real-world distribution shifts.

Appendix A Appendix

A.1 Connection to online learning

In Section 2 we motivated the update (2) as a way to adjust the size of our prediction sets in response to the realized historical miscoverage frequency. Alternatively, one could also derive (2) as an online gradient descent algorithm with respect to the pinball loss. To be more precise let

βt:=sup{β:Yt∈C^t​(β)},\beta_{t}:=\sup\{\beta:Y_{t}\in\hat{C}_{t}(\beta)\},

where we remark that C^t​(βt)\hat{C}_{t}(\beta_{t}) can be thought of as the smallest prediction set containing YtY_{t}. Additionally, define the pinball loss

ρα​(u)={α​u,u>0,−(1−α)​u,u≤0..\rho_{\alpha}(u)=\begin{cases}\alpha u,\ u>0,\\ -(1-\alpha)u,\ u\leq 0.\\ \end{cases}.

and consider the loss ℓ⁡(αt,βt)=ρα​(βt−αt)\ell(\alpha_{t},\beta_{t})=\rho_{\alpha}(\beta_{t}-\alpha_{t}). Then, one directly computes that

αt−γ​∂αtℓ⁡(αt,βt)=αt+γ⁡(α−𝟙αt>βt)=αt+γ⁡(α−errt).\alpha_{t}-\gamma\partial_{\alpha_{t}}\ell(\alpha_{t},\beta_{t})=\alpha_{t}+\gamma(\alpha-\mathbbm{1}_{\alpha_{t}>\beta_{t}})=\alpha_{t}+\gamma(\alpha-\text{err}_{t}).

Because the pinball loss is convex, this gradient descent update falls within a well understood class of algorithms that have been extensively studied in the online learning literature (see e.g. [17]). A standard analysis may then be to bound the regret of αt\alpha_{t} defined as

RegT:=∑t=1Tℓ⁡(αt,βt)−min⁡∑t=1Tβ⁡ℓ⁡(β,βt).\text{Reg}_{T}:=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell(\alpha_{t},\beta_{t})-\min_{\beta}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell(\beta,\beta_{t}).

Unfortunately, this notion of regret fails to capture our intuition that αt\alpha_{t} is adaptively tracking the moving target αt∗\alpha^{*}_{t}. Thus, we make the connection to online gradient descent only in passing and develop alternative theoretical tools in Section 4.

A.5 Existence of a stationary distribution for (𝜶𝒕,𝑨𝒕)\boldsymbol{(\alpha_{t},A_{t})}

In this section we give one simple example in which the Markov chain {(αt,At)}t∈ℕ\{(\alpha_{t},A_{t})\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}} will have a unique stationary distribution. The setting considered here is the same as the one described in Section 4.2.

Let αt\alpha_{t} be initialized with α1∈{α+k​γ​α:k∈ℤ}\alpha_{1}\in\{\alpha+k\gamma\alpha:k\in\mathbb{Z}\}. Assume that 𝒜\mathcal{A} is finite. Let PP be the transition matrix of {At}t∈ℕ\{A_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}} and assume that for all a1,a2∈𝒜a_{1},a_{2}\in\mathcal{A}, Pa1,a2=ℙ⁡(At+1=a2|At=a1)>0P_{a_{1},a_{2}}=\mathbb{P}(A_{t+1}=a_{2}|A_{t}=a_{1})>0. Assume that α\alpha satisfies α−1​(1−α)∈ℕ\alpha^{-1}(1-\alpha)\in\mathbb{N}. This will hold for common choices of α\alpha such as α=0.1\alpha=0.1 and α=0.05\alpha=0.05. Finally, assume that for all a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A} and all p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1), ℙ⁡(S⁡(Xt,Yt)≤Q^​(p)|A=a)∈(0,1)\mathbb{P}(S(X_{t},Y_{t})\leq\hat{Q}(p)|A=a)\in(0,1). This will occur for example when S⁡(Xt,Yt)|At=aS(X_{t},Y_{t})|A_{t}=a is supported on ℝ\mathbb{R} and Q^​(⋅)\hat{Q}(\cdot) is finite valued for all p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1).

We claim that in this case {(αt,At)}t∈ℕ\{(\alpha_{t},A_{t})\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}} has a unique stationary distribution. To prove this it is sufficient to show that this chain is irreducible and has a finite state space. To check that it has a finite state space it is sufficient to show that αt\alpha_{t} has a finite state space. We claim that with probability one we have that for all t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N}, αt∈{α+k​γ​α:k∈ℤ}\alpha_{t}\in\{\alpha+k\gamma\alpha:k\in\mathbb{Z}\}. To prove this we proceed by induction. The base case is given by our choice of α1\alpha_{1}. For the inductive step note that

αt∈{α+k​γ​α:k∈ℤ}\displaystyle\alpha_{t}\in\{\alpha+k\gamma\alpha:k\in\mathbb{Z}\}
⟹αt+1=αt+γ⁡(α−errt)={αt+γ​α, if errt=0,αt−γ​α​(α−1​(1−α)), if errt=1,∈{α+k​γ​α:k∈ℤ}.\displaystyle\implies\alpha_{t+1}=\alpha_{t}+\gamma(\alpha-\text{err}_{t})=\begin{cases}\alpha_{t}+\gamma\alpha,\text{ if }\text{err}_{t}=0,\\ \alpha_{t}-\gamma\alpha(\alpha^{-1}(1-\alpha)),\text{ if }\text{err}_{t}=1,\end{cases}\in\{\alpha+k\gamma\alpha:k\in\mathbb{Z}\}.

Since αt\alpha_{t} is also bounded (see Lemma 4.1) this implies that αt\alpha_{t} has a finite state space.

Finally, the fact that {(αt,At)}t∈ℕ\{(\alpha_{t},A_{t})\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}} is irreducible follows easily from our assumptions on {At}t∈ℕ\{A_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}}, Q^​(⋅)\hat{Q}(\cdot), and ℙ⁡(S⁡(Xt,Yt)≤Q^​(p)|A=a)\mathbb{P}(S(X_{t},Y_{t})\leq\hat{Q}(p)|A=a).

A.6 Additional information for Section 6

A.6.1 Dataset description

The county-level demographic characteristics used for prediction were the proportion of the total population that fell into each of the following race categories (either alone or in combination): black or African American, American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian, Native Hawaiian or other Pacific islander. In addition to this, we also used the proportion of the total population that was male, of Hispanic origin, and that fell within each of the age ranges 20-29, 30-44, 45-64, and 65+. Demographic information was obtained from 2019 estimates published by the United States Census Bureau and available at [5]. To supplement these demographic features we also used the median household income and the percentage of individuals with a bachelors degree or higher as covariates. Data on county-level median household incomes was based on 2019 estimates obtained from [7]. The percentage of individuals with a bachelors degree or higher was computed based on data collected during the years 2015-2019 and published at [6]. As an aside, we remark that we used 2019 estimates because this was the most recent year for which data was available.

Vote counts for the 2016 election were obtained from [14], while 2020 election data was taken from [25]. In total, matching covariate and election vote count data were obtained for 3111 counties.

A.6.2 Detailed prediction algorithm

Algorithm 1 below outlines the core conformal inference method used to predict election results. An R implementation of this algorithm as well as the core method outlined in Section 2.2 can be found at https://github.com/isgibbs/AdaptiveConformal.

A.7 Large deviation bounds for the error sequence

In this section we prove Theorem 4.1. So, throughout we define the sequences {αt}t∈ℕ\{\alpha_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}}, {errt}t∈ℕ\{\text{err}_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}}, and {At}t∈ℕ\{A_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}} as in Section 4.2 and we assume that {(αt,At)}t∈ℕ\{(\alpha_{t},A_{t})\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}} is a stationary Markov chain from which it follows immediately that {(αt,At,errt)}t∈ℕ\{(\alpha_{t},A_{t},\text{err}_{t})\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}} is also stationary. Additionally, we assume that Q^​(⋅)\hat{Q}(\cdot) and S⁡(⋅)S(\cdot) are fixed functions such that Q^​(⋅)\hat{Q}(\cdot) is non-decreasing with Q^​(x)=−∞\hat{Q}(x)=-\infty for all x<0x<0 and Q^​(x)=∞\hat{Q}(x)=\infty for all x>1x>1. The proof of Theorem 4.1 will rely on the following lemmas.

Lemma A.1

Let f:ℝ→ℝf:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} and g:ℝ→ℝg:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} be bounded functions such that either

  1. 1.

    ff is non-increasing and gg is non-decreasing,

  2. 2.

    or ff is non-decreasing and gg is non-increasing.

Then, for any random variable YY

𝔼⁡[f⁡(Y)​g​(Y)]≤𝔼⁡[f⁡(Y)]​𝔼​[g⁡(Y)].\mathbb{E}[f(Y)g(Y)]\leq\mathbb{E}[f(Y)]\mathbb{E}[g(Y)].

The proof of this result is straightforward and can be found in Section A.10.

Lemma A.2

For any λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R} and t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N} we have that

𝔼⁡[∏s=1texp⁡(λ⁡(errs−𝔼⁡[errs|As]))]≤exp⁡(λ2/2)​𝔼​[∏s=1t−1exp⁡(λ⁡(errs−𝔼⁡[errs|As]))].\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{s=1}^{t}\exp(\lambda(\textup{err}_{s}-\mathbb{E}[\textup{err}_{s}|A_{s}]))\right]\leq\exp(\lambda^{2}/2)\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{s=1}^{t-1}\exp(\lambda(\textup{err}_{s}-\mathbb{E}[\textup{err}_{s}|A_{s}]))\right]. (8)
Proof:

By conditioning on α1\alpha_{1} and A1,…,AtA_{1},\dots,A_{t} on both the left and right-hand side of (8) we may view these quantities as fixed. Thus, while for readability we do not denote this conditioning explicitly, the following calculations should be read as conditional on α1\alpha_{1} and A1,…,AtA_{1},\dots,A_{t}. Then,

𝔼⁡[∏s=1texp⁡(λ⁡(errs−𝔼⁡[errs|As]))]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{s=1}^{t}\exp(\lambda(\text{err}_{s}-\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{s}|A_{s}]))\right]
=𝔼[∏s=1t−1exp(λ(errs−𝔼[errs|As]))𝔼[exp(λ(errt−𝔼[errt|At]))|err1,…,errt−1]].\displaystyle\ \ \ \ \ \ =\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{s=1}^{t-1}\exp(\lambda(\text{err}_{s}-\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{s}|A_{s}]))\mathbb{E}\bigg[\exp(\lambda(\text{err}_{t}-\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{t}|A_{t}]))\bigg|\text{err}_{1},\dots,\text{err}_{t-1}\bigg]\right].

Recall that αt=α1+γ​∑s=1t−1(α−errs)\alpha_{t}=\alpha_{1}+\gamma\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}(\alpha-\text{err}_{s}) is a deterministic function of α1\alpha_{1} and ∑s=1t−1errs\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\text{err}_{s}. So, we may define the functions f⁡(∑s=1t−1errs)=∏s=1t−1exp⁡(λ⁡(errs−𝔼⁡[errs|As]))f(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\text{err}_{s})=\prod_{s=1}^{t-1}\exp(\lambda(\text{err}_{s}-\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{s}|A_{s}])) and

g⁡(∑s=1t−1errs)\displaystyle g(\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\text{err}_{s}) :=𝔼[exp(λ(errt−𝔼[errt|At]))|err1,…,errt−1]\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}\left[\exp(\lambda(\text{err}_{t}-\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{t}|A_{t}]))|\text{err}_{1},\dots,\text{err}_{t-1}\right]
=PAt​(S⁡(Xt,Yt)≤Q^​(1−αt))​exp⁡(−λ​𝔼​[errt|At])\displaystyle=P_{A_{t}}(S(X_{t},Y_{t})\leq\hat{Q}(1-\alpha_{t}))\exp(-\lambda\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{t}|A_{t}])
+(1−PAt​(S⁡(Xt,Yt)≤Q^​(1−αt)))​exp⁡(λ⁡(1−𝔼⁡[errt|At])),\displaystyle\ \ \ \ +(1-P_{A_{t}}(S(X_{t},Y_{t})\leq\hat{Q}(1-\alpha_{t})))\exp(\lambda(1-\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{t}|A_{t}])),

where we emphasize that on the last line AtA_{t} and αt\alpha_{t} should be viewed as fixed quantities. Now, since αt\alpha_{t} is monotonically decreasing in ∑s=1t−1errs\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\text{err}_{s} it should be clear that if λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 then gg is non-increasing (resp. non-decreasing for λ<0\lambda<0) and ff is non-decreasing (resp. non-increasing for λ<0\lambda<0). So, by Lemma A.1 we have that

𝔼[∏s=1t−1exp(λ(errs−𝔼[errs|As]))𝔼[exp(λ(errt−𝔼[errt|At]))|err1,…,errt−1]]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{s=1}^{t-1}\exp(\lambda(\text{err}_{s}-\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{s}|A_{s}]))\mathbb{E}\bigg[\exp(\lambda(\text{err}_{t}-\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{t}|A_{t}]))\bigg|\text{err}_{1},\dots,\text{err}_{t-1}\bigg]\right]
≤𝔼[∏s=1t−1exp(λ(errs−𝔼[errs|As]))]𝔼[𝔼[exp(λ(errt−𝔼[errt|At]))|err1,…,errt−1]]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{s=1}^{t-1}\exp(\lambda(\text{err}_{s}-\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{s}|A_{s}]))\right]\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}\bigg[\exp(\lambda(\text{err}_{t}-\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{t}|A_{t}]))\bigg|\text{err}_{1},\dots,\text{err}_{t-1}\bigg]\right]
=𝔼⁡[∏s=1t−1exp⁡(λ⁡(errs−𝔼⁡[errs|As]))]​𝔼​[exp⁡(λ⁡(errt−𝔼⁡[errt|At]))]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{s=1}^{t-1}\exp(\lambda(\text{err}_{s}-\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{s}|A_{s}]))\right]\mathbb{E}[\exp(\lambda(\text{err}_{t}-\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{t}|A_{t}]))]
≤𝔼⁡[∏s=1t−1exp⁡(λ⁡(errs−𝔼⁡[errs|As]))]​exp⁡(λ2/2),\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{s=1}^{t-1}\exp(\lambda(\text{err}_{s}-\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{s}|A_{s}]))\right]\exp(\lambda^{2}/2),

where the last inequality follows by Hoeffding’s lemma (see Lemma A.5). □\square

The final result we will need in order to prove Theorem 4.1 is a large deviation bound for Markov chains.

Definition A.1

Let {Xi}i∈ℕ⊆𝒳\{X_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\mathcal{X} be a Markov chain with transition kernel PP and stationary distribution π\pi. Define the inner product space

L2​(𝒳,π)={h:∫𝒳h​(x)2​π​(𝑑x)<∞}L^{2}(\mathcal{X},\pi)=\left\{h:\int_{\mathcal{X}}h(x)^{2}\pi(dx)<\infty\right\}

with inner product

⟨h1,h2⟩π=∫𝒳h1​(x)​h2​(x)​π​(𝑑x).\langle h_{1},h_{2}\rangle_{\pi}=\int_{\mathcal{X}}h_{1}(x)h_{2}(x)\pi(dx).

For any h∈L2​(𝒳,π)h\in L^{2}(\mathcal{X},\pi), let

L2​(𝒳,π)∋P​h:=∫h⁡(y)​P​(⋅,𝑑y).L^{2}(\mathcal{X},\pi)\ni Ph:=\int h(y)P(\cdot,dy).

Then, we say that {Xi}i∈ℕ\{X_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}} has non-zero absolute spectral gap 1−η1-\eta if

η:=sup{⟨P​h,P​h⟩π:⟨h,h⟩π=1,∫𝒳h(x)π(dx)=0}<1.\eta:=\sup\left\{\sqrt{\langle Ph,Ph\rangle_{\pi}}:\langle h,h\rangle_{\pi}=1,\ \int_{\mathcal{X}}h(x)\pi(dx)=0\right\}<1.
Theorem A.1 (Theorem 1 in [19])

Let {Xi}i∈ℕ⊆𝒳\{X_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\mathcal{X} be a stationary Markov chain with invariant distribution π\pi and non-zero absolute spectral gap 1−η>01-\eta>0. Let fi:𝒳→[−C,C]f_{i}:\mathcal{X}\to[-C,C] be a sequence of functions with π⁡(fi)=0\pi(f_{i})=0 and define σ2:=∑i=1nπ⁡(fi2)/n\sigma^{2}:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\pi(f_{i}^{2})/n. Then, for ∀ϵ>0\forall\epsilon>0,

ℙπ​(1n​∑i=1nfi​(Xi)≥ϵ)≤exp⁡(−n⁡(1−η)​ϵ2/2(1+η)​σ2+5​C​ϵ).\mathbb{P}_{\pi}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}(X_{i})\geq\epsilon\right)\leq\exp\left(-\frac{n(1-\eta)\epsilon^{2}/2}{(1+\eta)\sigma^{2}+5C\epsilon}\right).

Finally, we are ready to prove Theorem 4.1.

Proof:

[Proof of Theorem 4.1.] Write

ℙ⁡(|1T​∑t=1Terrt−α|>ϵ)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\text{err}_{t}-\alpha\right|>\epsilon\right) (9)
≤ℙ⁡(|1T​∑t=1Terrt−𝔼⁡[errt|At]|>ϵ/2)+ℙ⁡(|1T​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[errt|At]−α|>ϵ/2)\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\text{err}_{t}-\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{t}|A_{t}]\right|>\epsilon/2\right)+\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{t}|A_{t}]-\alpha\right|>\epsilon/2\right) (10)

By applying lemma A.2 inductively we have that for all λ>0\lambda>0,

ℙ⁡(1T​∑t=1Terrt−𝔼⁡[errt|At]>ϵ/2)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\text{err}_{t}-\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{t}|A_{t}]>\epsilon/2\right) ≤exp(−Tλϵ/2)𝔼[∏t=1Texp(λ(errt−𝔼[errt|At]))]\displaystyle\leq\exp(-T\lambda\epsilon/2)\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{t=1}^{T}\exp(\lambda(\text{err}_{t}-\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{t}|A_{t}]))\right]
≤exp(−Tλϵ/2)exp(Tλ2/2),\displaystyle\leq\exp(-T\lambda\epsilon/2)\exp(T\lambda^{2}/2),

with an identical bound on the left tail. Choosing λ=ϵ/2\lambda=\epsilon/2 gives the bound

ℙ(|1T∑t=1Terrt−𝔼[errt|At]|>ϵ/2)≤2exp(−Tϵ2/8).\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\text{err}_{t}-\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{t}|A_{t}]\right|>\epsilon/2\right)\leq 2\exp(-T\epsilon^{2}/8).

On the other hand, the second term in (10) can be bounded directly using Theorem A.1. □\square

A.8 Approximate marginal coverage

In this section we prove Theorem 4.2.

Proof:

[Proof of Theorem 4.2] Our proof follows similar steps to those presented in previous works on stochastic gradient descent under distribution shift [9, 35]. First, note that

(αt+1−αAt∗)2=(αt−αAt∗)2+2​γ​(α−errt)​(αt−αAt∗)+γ2​(α−errt)2.(\alpha_{t+1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}})^{2}=(\alpha_{t}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}})^{2}+2\gamma(\alpha-\text{err}_{t})(\alpha_{t}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}})+\gamma^{2}(\alpha-\text{err}_{t})^{2}.

Now recalling that M⁡(αAt∗|At)=αM(\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}}|A_{t})=\alpha, we find that

−𝔼⁡[(α−errt)​(αt−αAt∗)]\displaystyle-\mathbb{E}[(\alpha-\text{err}_{t})(\alpha_{t}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}})] =𝔼[𝔼[(errt−α)(αt−αAt∗)|At,αt]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[(\text{err}_{t}-\alpha)(\alpha_{t}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}})|A_{t},\alpha_{t}]]
=𝔼⁡[(M⁡(αt|At)−M⁡(αAt∗|At))​(αt−αAt∗)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[(M(\alpha_{t}|A_{t})-M(\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}}|A_{t}))(\alpha_{t}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}})]
≥1L​𝔼​[(M⁡(αt|At)−M⁡(αAt∗|At))2]\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{L}\mathbb{E}[(M(\alpha_{t}|A_{t})-M(\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}}|A_{t}))^{2}]
=1L​𝔼​[(M⁡(αt|At)−α)2].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{L}\mathbb{E}[(M(\alpha_{t}|A_{t})-\alpha)^{2}].

Thus it follows that

2​γ​L−1​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[(M⁡(αt|At)−α)2]≤∑t=1T𝔼⁡[(αt−αAt∗)2−(αt+1−αAt∗)2+γ2​(α−errt)2]\displaystyle 2\gamma L^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[(M(\alpha_{t}|A_{t})-\alpha)^{2}]\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{t}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}})^{2}-(\alpha_{t+1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}})^{2}+\gamma^{2}(\alpha-\text{err}_{t})^{2}]
≤∑t=1T𝔼⁡[(αt+1−αAt+1∗)2−(αt+1−αAt∗)2]+𝔼⁡[(α1−αA1∗)2]+γ2​T\displaystyle\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{t+1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t+1}})^{2}-(\alpha_{t+1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}})^{2}]+\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{1}})^{2}]+\gamma^{2}T
≤∑t=1T𝔼⁡[2​αt+1​(αAt∗−αAt+1∗)]+(αAT+1∗)2+𝔼⁡[(α1−αA1∗)2]+γ2​T\displaystyle\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[2\alpha_{t+1}(\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t+1}})]+(\alpha^{*}_{A_{T+1}})^{2}+\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{1}})^{2}]+\gamma^{2}T
≤∑t=1T2​(1+γ)​𝔼​[|αAt+1∗−αAt∗|]+(αAT+1∗)2+𝔼⁡[(α1−αA1∗)2]+γ2​T,\displaystyle\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}2(1+\gamma)\mathbb{E}[|\alpha^{*}_{A_{t+1}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}}|]+(\alpha^{*}_{A_{T+1}})^{2}+\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{1}})^{2}]+\gamma^{2}T,

where the last inequality follows from Lemma 4.1. So, re-arranging we get the inequality

1T​∑t=1T𝔼⁡[(M⁡(αt|At)−α)2]\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}[(M(\alpha_{t}|A_{t})-\alpha)^{2}]
≤L2​T​γ​(∑t=1T2​(1+γ)​𝔼​[|αAt+1∗−αAt∗|]+(αAT+1∗)2+𝔼⁡[(α1−αA1∗)2]+γ2​T).\displaystyle\leq\frac{L}{2T\gamma}\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T}2(1+\gamma)\mathbb{E}[|\alpha^{*}_{A_{t+1}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}}|]+(\alpha^{*}_{A_{T+1}})^{2}+\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{1}})^{2}]+\gamma^{2}T\right).

Finally, since {(At,αt)}t∈ℕ\{(A_{t},\alpha_{t})\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}} is stationary we may let T→∞T\to\infty to get that

𝔼⁡[(M⁡(αt|At)−α)2]≤L⁡(1+γ)γ​𝔼​[|αAt+1∗−αAt∗|]+L​γ2\mathbb{E}[(M(\alpha_{t}|A_{t})-\alpha)^{2}]\leq\frac{L(1+\gamma)}{\gamma}\mathbb{E}[|\alpha^{*}_{A_{t+1}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}}|]+\frac{L\gamma}{2}

as claimed. □\square

A.9 Bounds on 𝑩\boldsymbol{B} and 𝝈𝑩𝟐\boldsymbol{\sigma^{2}_{B}}

In this section we bound the constants BB and σB2\sigma^{2}_{B} appearing in the statement of Theorem 4.1. Let

ϵ1=supk∈{0,1,2,…}supa∈𝒜𝔼⁡[|αAT−k∗−αAT−k−1∗||AT=a]\displaystyle\epsilon_{1}=\sup_{k\in\{0,1,2,\dots\}}\sup_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\mathbb{E}[|\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-k}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-k-1}}||A_{T}=a]
and ϵ2=supk∈{0,1,2,…}supa∈𝒜𝔼⁡[(αAT−k∗−αAT−k−1∗)2|AT=a].\displaystyle\epsilon_{2}=\sup_{k\in\{0,1,2,\dots\}}\sup_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\mathbb{E}[(\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-k}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-k-1}})^{2}|A_{T}=a].

Then, our main result is Lemma A.4 which shows that

B≤C⁡(γ+γ−1​(ϵ1+ϵ2)) and σB2≤B2,B\leq C(\gamma+\gamma^{-1}(\epsilon_{1}+\epsilon_{2}))\ \ \ \text{ and }\ \ \ \sigma^{2}_{B}\leq B^{2}, (11)

where the constant CC depends on how close M(⋅|a)M(\cdot|a) is to the ideal linear function M⁡(p|a)=pM(p|a)=p.

Plugging (11) into Theorem 4.1 gives a concentration inequality for |T−1​∑t=1Terrt−α||T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\text{err}_{t}-\alpha|. In particular, suppose we use an optimal stepsize of γ∝ϵ1\gamma\propto\sqrt{\epsilon_{1}}. Then, combining (11) with Theorem 4.1 roughly tells us that

|1T​∑t=1Terrt−α|≤O⁡(max⁡{1T,ϵ1T⁡(1−η),ϵ1T⁡(1−η)}).\left|\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\text{err}_{t}-\alpha\right|\leq O\left(\max\left\{\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}},\frac{\sqrt{\epsilon_{1}}}{\sqrt{T(1-\eta)}},\frac{\sqrt{\epsilon_{1}}}{T(1-\eta)}\right\}\right). (12)

As a comparison it may be instructive to note that the more naive bound given in Proposition 4.1 can be written as

|1T​∑t=1Terrt−α|≤O⁡(1T​γ)=O⁡(1T​ϵ1).\left|\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\text{err}_{t}-\alpha\right|\leq O\left(\frac{1}{T\gamma}\right)=O\left(\frac{1}{T\sqrt{\epsilon_{1}}}\right). (13)

A sharp reader may notice that the naive bound given in (13) actually goes to 0 faster in TT than the HMM-based bound shown in (12). While this is true, the bound (13) has the highly undesirable property of increasing in 1/ϵ11/\sqrt{\epsilon_{1}}, i.e. the bound increases as the size of the distribution shift decreases. On the other hand, the HMM-based bound has the more intuitive property of decreasing with the distribution shift.

The only remaining issue is to determine the size of ϵ1/(1−η)\sqrt{\epsilon_{1}/(1-\eta)}. To provide some insight into this quantity note that there are two main regimes in which we expect |T−1​∑t=1Terrt−α||T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\text{err}_{t}-\alpha| to be small:

  1. 1.

    Environments in which the state AtA_{t} changes frequently, but |αAt+1∗−αAt∗||\alpha^{*}_{A_{t+1}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}}| is always small. In this case it is reasonable to expect 1−η1-\eta to not be too small and so we anticipate that (12) will give a reasonable bound.

  2. 2.

    Environments in which the state changes very infrequently. In this case {At}t∈ℕ\{A_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}} will mix slowly and so we expect 1−η1-\eta to be quite small. Additionally, we also have that αAt+1∗=αAt∗\alpha^{*}_{A_{t+1}}=\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}} a large proportion of the time and thus ϵ1\epsilon_{1} will also be small. As a result, it is not immediately clear what (12) tells us about |T−1​∑t=1Terrt−α||T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\text{err}_{t}-\alpha|. Below we give one simple example that demonstrates that (12) can also be a reasonable bound in this instance.

Example A.1

Let {At}t∈ℕ\{A_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}} be the Markov chain with states {1,…,n}\{1,\dots,n\} and transition matrix

P=(p−1−pn−1)​I+1−pn−1​11T,P=\left(p-\frac{1-p}{n-1}\right)I+\frac{1-p}{n-1}11^{T},

where p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1] is taken to be very close to 1. Let Δ:=maxi≠j⁡|αi∗−αj∗|\Delta:=\max_{i\neq j}|\alpha^{*}_{i}-\alpha^{*}_{j}|. Then, we have that ϵ1,ϵ2≤Δ⁡(1−p)\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2}\leq\Delta(1-p). Moreover, note that this chain has spectral gap 1−η≅1−p1-\eta\cong 1-p. Thus, (12) simplifies to

|1T​∑t=1Terrt−α|≤O⁡(max⁡{1T,ΔT​1−p}).\left|\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\text{err}_{t}-\alpha\right|\leq O\left(\max\left\{\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}},\frac{\sqrt{\Delta}}{T\sqrt{1-p}}\right\}\right). (14)

In particular, for T>Δ/(1−p)T>\Delta/(1-p) we find that the error sequence concentrates at a rate of O⁡(1/T)O(1/\sqrt{T}), which is consistent with the behaviour of an i.i.d. Bernoulli sequence. Finally, to understand this restriction on TT note that given a starting state j∈{1,…,n}j\in\{1,\dots,n\} we expect αt\alpha_{t} to contract towards αj∗\alpha_{j}^{*} at a rate of (1−γ)(1-\gamma) and therefore to have that

1T​∑t=1T|αt−αj∗|∝1T​∑t=1T(1−γ)t−1​|α1−αj∗|≤ΔT​γ=ΔT​1−p,\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}|\alpha_{t}-\alpha^{*}_{j}|\propto\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}(1-\gamma)^{t-1}|\alpha_{1}-\alpha^{*}_{j}|\leq\frac{\Delta}{T\gamma}=\frac{\sqrt{\Delta}}{T\sqrt{1-p}},

where here we assumed that α1∈{α1∗,…,αn∗}\alpha_{1}\in\{\alpha^{*}_{1},\dots,\alpha^{*}_{n}\}. Thus, the second term in the maximum in (14) can be seen as accounting for the rate of covergence of αt\alpha_{t} to αj∗\alpha^{*}_{j} during the time that the Markov chain is in state jj and given that α1\alpha_{1} starts at some αi∗\alpha^{*}_{i}, 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n.

We now derive (11).

Lemma A.3

Assume that ∃0<c<1/(2​γ)\exists 0<c<1/(2\gamma) such that for all a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A} and all p∈[−γ,1+γ]p\in[-\gamma,1+\gamma],

|M⁡(p|a)−M⁡(αa∗|a)|≥c​|p−αa∗|.|M(p|a)-M(\alpha^{*}_{a}|a)|\geq c|p-\alpha^{*}_{a}|.

Then, for all a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, k∈{0,1,2,…}k\in\{0,1,2,\dots\}, and T∈ℕT\in\mathbb{N}

𝔼⁡[(α1−αA1∗)2|A1+k=a]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{1}})^{2}|A_{1+k}=a]
≤(1−2​c​γ)T−1​𝔼​[(α1−αA1∗)2|AT+k=a]\displaystyle\leq(1-2c\gamma)^{T-1}\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{1}})^{2}|A_{T+k}=a]
+∑t=2T(1−2cγ)T−t(γ2+2(1+γ)𝔼[|αAt−1∗−αAt∗||AT+k=a]+𝔼[(αAt−1∗−αAt∗)2|AT+k=a]).\displaystyle+\sum_{t=2}^{T}(1-2c\gamma)^{T-t}\bigg(\gamma^{2}+2(1+\gamma)\mathbb{E}[|\alpha^{*}_{A_{t-1}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}}||A_{T+k}=a]+\mathbb{E}[(\alpha^{*}_{A_{t-1}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}})^{2}|A_{T+k}=a]\bigg).

Furthermore, if we assume that ∀a∈𝒜\forall a\in\mathcal{A} and k∈{0,1,2,…}k\in\{0,1,2,\dots\},

𝔼⁡[|αAt−k∗−αAt−k−1∗||At=a]≤ϵ1​ and ​𝔼​[(αAt−k∗−αAt−k−1∗)2|At=a]≤ϵ2,\mathbb{E}[|\alpha^{*}_{A_{t-k}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t-k-1}}||A_{t}=a]\leq\epsilon_{1}\text{ and }\mathbb{E}[(\alpha^{*}_{A_{t-k}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t-k-1}})^{2}|A_{t}=a]\leq\epsilon_{2},

then we find that

𝔼⁡[(α1−αA1∗)2|A1+k=a]≤12​c​γ​(γ2+2​(1+γ)​ϵ1+ϵ2).\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{1}})^{2}|A_{1+k}=a]\leq\frac{1}{2c\gamma}\left(\gamma^{2}+2(1+\gamma)\epsilon_{1}+\epsilon_{2}\right).
Proof:

Fix any T∈ℕT\in\mathbb{N}. Since {(αt,At)}t∈ℕ\{(\alpha_{t},A_{t})\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}} is stationary we have that

𝔼⁡[(α1−αA1∗)2|A1+k]=𝔼⁡[(αT−αAT∗)2|AT+k].\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{1}})^{2}|A_{1+k}]=\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{T}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T}})^{2}|A_{T+k}].

Now note that

𝔼⁡[(αT−αAT∗)2|AT+k]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{T}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T}})^{2}|A_{T+k}] =𝔼⁡[(αT−αAT−1∗)2|AT+k]+2​𝔼​[(αT−αAT−1∗)​(αAT−1∗−αAT∗)|AT+k]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{T}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}})^{2}|A_{T+k}]+2\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{T}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}})(\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T}})|A_{T+k}]
+𝔼⁡[(αAT−1∗−αAT∗)2|AT+k]\displaystyle\ \ \ \ +\mathbb{E}[(\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T}})^{2}|A_{T+k}]
≤𝔼⁡[(αT−αAT−1∗)2|AT+k]+2​(1+γ)​𝔼​[|αAT−1∗−αAT∗||AT+k]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{T}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}})^{2}|A_{T+k}]+2(1+\gamma)\mathbb{E}[|\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T}}||A_{T+k}]
+𝔼⁡[(αAT−1∗−αAT∗)2|AT+k],\displaystyle\ \ \ \ +\mathbb{E}[(\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T}})^{2}|A_{T+k}],

where on the last line we have applied Lemma 4.1. The first term above can be bounded as

𝔼⁡[(αT−αAT−1∗)2|AT+k]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{T}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}})^{2}|A_{T+k}]
≤𝔼⁡[(αT−1−αAT−1∗)2|AT+k]+2​𝔼​[γ⁡(α−errT−1)​(αT−1−αAT−1∗)|AT+k]+γ2,\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{T-1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}})^{2}|A_{T+k}]+2\mathbb{E}[\gamma(\alpha-\text{err}_{T-1})(\alpha_{T-1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}})|A_{T+k}]+\gamma^{2},

where we additionally have that

𝔼⁡[(α−errT)​(αT−1−αAT−1∗)|AT+k]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(\alpha-\text{err}_{T})(\alpha_{T-1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}})|A_{T+k}]
=𝔼[(α−𝔼[errT−1|AT−1,αT−1,AT+k])(αT−1−αAT−1∗)|AT+k]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[(\alpha-\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{T-1}|A_{T-1},\alpha_{T-1},A_{T+k}])(\alpha_{T-1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}})|A_{T+k}]
=𝔼⁡[(M⁡(αAT−1∗|AT1)−M⁡(αT−1|AT−1))​(αT−1−αAT−1∗)|AT+k]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[(M(\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}}|A_{T_{1}})-M(\alpha_{T-1}|A_{T-1}))(\alpha_{T-1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}})|A_{T+k}]
≤−c​𝔼​[(αT−1−αAT−1∗)2|AT+k].\displaystyle\leq-c\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{T-1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}})^{2}|A_{T+k}].

Whence,

𝔼⁡[(αT−αAT−1∗)2|AT+k]≤(1−2​c​γ)​𝔼​[(αT−1−αAT−1∗)2|AT+k]+γ2,\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{T}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}})^{2}|A_{T+k}]\leq(1-2c\gamma)\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{T-1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}})^{2}|A_{T+k}]+\gamma^{2},

and plugging this into our first inequality yields

𝔼⁡[(αT−αAT∗)2|AT+k]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{T}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T}})^{2}|A_{T+k}] ≤(1−2​c​γ)​𝔼​[(αT−1−αAT−1∗)2|AT+k]+γ2\displaystyle\leq(1-2c\gamma)\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{T-1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}})^{2}|A_{T+k}]+\gamma^{2}
+2​(1+γ)​𝔼​[|αAT−1∗−αAT∗||AT+k]+𝔼⁡[(αAT−1∗−αAT∗)2|AT+k].\displaystyle\ \ \ \ +2(1+\gamma)\mathbb{E}[|\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T}}||A_{T+k}]+\mathbb{E}[(\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T}})^{2}|A_{T+k}].

Repeating this argument inductively gives

𝔼⁡[(αT−αAT∗)2|AT+k=a]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{T}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T}})^{2}|A_{T+k}=a]
≤(1−2​c​γ)T−1​𝔼​[(α1−αA1∗)2|AT+k=a]\displaystyle\leq(1-2c\gamma)^{T-1}\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{1}})^{2}|A_{T+k}=a]
+∑t=2T(1−2cγ)T−t(γ2+2(1+γ)𝔼[|αAt−1∗−αAt∗||AT+k=a]+𝔼[(αAt−1∗−αAt∗)2|AT+k=a]).\displaystyle+\sum_{t=2}^{T}(1-2c\gamma)^{T-t}\bigg(\gamma^{2}+2(1+\gamma)\mathbb{E}[|\alpha^{*}_{A_{t-1}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}}||A_{T+k}=a]+\mathbb{E}[(\alpha^{*}_{A_{t-1}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}})^{2}|A_{T+k}=a]\bigg).

The final part of the lemma follows by sending T→∞T\to\infty. □\square

Lemma A.4

Assume that for all a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A} and p∈[−γ,1+γ]p\in[-\gamma,1+\gamma], M(⋅|a)M(\cdot|a) admits the second order Taylor expansion

M⁡(p|a)−M⁡(αa∗|a)=Ca1​(p−αa∗)+Cp,a2​(p−αa∗)2,M(p|a)-M(\alpha^{*}_{a}|a)=C^{1}_{a}(p-\alpha^{*}_{a})+C^{2}_{p,a}(p-\alpha^{*}_{a})^{2},

where 0<c1≤Ca1≤C1<1/γ0<c_{1}\leq C^{1}_{a}\leq C_{1}<1/\gamma and |Cp,a2|≤C2|C^{2}_{p,a}|\leq C_{2}. Then, for all T∈ℕT\in\mathbb{N} and a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A},

|𝔼⁡[err1|A1=a]−α|\displaystyle\left|\mathbb{E}[\textup{err}_{1}|A_{1}=a]-\alpha\right| ≤C1​(1−γ​c1)T−1​𝔼​[|α1−αA1∗||AT=a]\displaystyle\leq C_{1}(1-\gamma c_{1})^{T-1}\mathbb{E}[|\alpha_{1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{1}}||A_{T}=a]
+∑t=1T−1C1C2γ(1−c1γ)T−t−1𝔼[(αt−αAt∗)2|AT=a]\displaystyle+\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}C_{1}C_{2}\gamma(1-c_{1}\gamma)^{T-t-1}\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{t}-\alpha_{A^{*}_{t}})^{2}|A_{T}=a]
+∑t=1T−1C1(1−c1γ)T−t−1𝔼[|αAt+1∗−αAt∗||AT]+C2𝔼[(αT−αAT∗)2|AT=a].\displaystyle+\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}C_{1}(1-c_{1}\gamma)^{T-t-1}\mathbb{E}[|\alpha^{*}_{A_{t+1}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{t}}||A_{T}]+C_{2}\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{T}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T}})^{2}|A_{T}=a].

Furthermore, suppose the assumptions of Lemma A.3 hold and that ∀a∈𝒜\forall a\in\mathcal{A} and k∈{0,1,2,…}k\in\{0,1,2,\dots\},

𝔼⁡[|αAT−k∗−αAT−k−1∗||AT=a]≤ϵ1​ and ​𝔼​[(αAT−k∗−αAT−k−1∗)2|AT=a]≤ϵ2.\mathbb{E}[|\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-k}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-k-1}}||A_{T}=a]\leq\epsilon_{1}\text{ and }\mathbb{E}[(\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-k}}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-k-1}})^{2}|A_{T}=a]\leq\epsilon_{2}.

Then ∀a∈𝒜\forall a\in\mathcal{A},

|𝔼⁡[err1|A1=a]−α|≤(C1​C2​1c1+C2)​12​c​γ​(γ2+2​(1+γ)​ϵ1+ϵ2)+C1c1​γ​ϵ1.\left|\mathbb{E}[\textup{err}_{1}|A_{1}=a]-\alpha\right|\leq\left(C_{1}C_{2}\frac{1}{c_{1}}+C_{2}\right)\frac{1}{2c\gamma}(\gamma^{2}+2(1+\gamma)\epsilon_{1}+\epsilon_{2})+\frac{C_{1}}{c_{1}\gamma}\epsilon_{1}.
Proof:

Fix any T∈ℕT\in\mathbb{N}. Since {(errt,At)}t∈ℕ\{(\text{err}_{t},A_{t})\}_{t\in\mathbb{N}} is stationary we have that

𝔼⁡[err1|A1=a]=𝔼⁡[errT|AT=a].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{1}|A_{1}=a]=\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{T}|A_{T}=a].

Then, by Taylor expanding M(⋅|AT)M(\cdot|A_{T}) we find that

|𝔼⁡[errT|AT=a]−α|=|𝔼⁡[M⁡(αT|AT)−M⁡(αAT∗|AT)|AT]|\displaystyle\left|\mathbb{E}[\text{err}_{T}|A_{T}=a]-\alpha\right|=\left|\mathbb{E}[M(\alpha_{T}|A_{T})-M(\alpha^{*}_{A_{T}}|A_{T})|A_{T}]\right|
≤|𝔼⁡[CAT1​(αT−αAT∗)|AT]|+𝔼⁡[CαT,AT2​(αT−αAT∗)2|AT]\displaystyle\leq\left|\mathbb{E}[C^{1}_{A_{T}}(\alpha_{T}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T}})|A_{T}]\right|+\mathbb{E}[C_{\alpha_{T},A_{T}}^{2}(\alpha_{T}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T}})^{2}|A_{T}]
≤|𝔼⁡[CAT1​(αT−αAT∗)|AT]|+C2​𝔼​[(αT−αAT∗)2|AT].\displaystyle\leq\left|\mathbb{E}[C^{1}_{A_{T}}(\alpha_{T}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T}})|A_{T}]\right|+C_{2}\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{T}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T}})^{2}|A_{T}].

The first term above can be further bounded as

|𝔼⁡[CAT1​(αT−αAT∗)|AT]|\displaystyle\left|\mathbb{E}[C^{1}_{A_{T}}(\alpha_{T}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T}})|A_{T}]\right|
=|𝔼⁡[CAT1​(αT−1+γ⁡(α−errT−1)−αAT−1∗)|AT]+𝔼⁡[CAT1​(αAT−1∗−αAT∗)|AT]|\displaystyle=\left|\mathbb{E}[C^{1}_{A_{T}}(\alpha_{T-1}+\gamma(\alpha-\text{err}_{T-1})-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}})|A_{T}]+\mathbb{E}[C^{1}_{A_{T}}(\alpha_{A_{T-1}}^{*}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T}})|A_{T}]\right|
≤|𝔼⁡[CAT1​(αT−1−αAT−1∗)]+γ​𝔼​[CAT1​(M⁡(αAT−1∗|AT−1)−M⁡(αT−1|AT−1))|AT]|\displaystyle\leq\left|\mathbb{E}[C_{A_{T}}^{1}(\alpha_{T-1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}})]+\gamma\mathbb{E}[C^{1}_{A_{T}}(M(\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}}|A_{T-1})-M(\alpha_{T-1}|A_{T-1}))|A_{T}]\right|
+C1​𝔼​[|αAT−1∗−αAT∗||AT]\displaystyle\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ +C_{1}\mathbb{E}[|\alpha_{A_{T-1}}^{*}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T}}||A_{T}]
=|𝔼⁡[CAT1​(1−γ​CAT−11)​(αT−1−αAT−1∗)|AT]|+C1​C2​γ​𝔼​[(αT−1−αAT−1∗)2|AT]\displaystyle=\left|\mathbb{E}[C^{1}_{A_{T}}(1-\gamma C^{1}_{A_{T-1}})(\alpha_{T-1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}})|A_{T}]\right|+C_{1}C_{2}\gamma\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{T-1}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T-1}})^{2}|A_{T}]
+C1​𝔼​[|αAT−1∗−αAT∗||AT].\displaystyle\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ +C_{1}\mathbb{E}[|\alpha_{A_{T-1}}^{*}-\alpha^{*}_{A_{T}}||A_{T}].

The desired result follows by repeating this process inductively. Finally, the last part of the Lemma follows by sending T→∞T\to\infty and applying the result of Lemma A.3.

□\square

As a final aside we remark that in the main text we claimed that in the ideal case where M⁡(p|a)=pM(p|a)=p for all p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1] this bound can be replaced by

|𝔼⁡[err1|A1=a]−α|≤2​(γ+γ−1​ϵ1).\left|\mathbb{E}[\textup{err}_{1}|A_{1}=a]-\alpha\right|\leq 2(\gamma+\gamma^{-1}\epsilon_{1}).

This can be justified by using the fact that in this case we have that for all p∈[−γ,1+γ]p\in[-\gamma,1+\gamma]

M⁡(p|a)−M⁡(αa∗|a)=(p−αa∗)+Cp,a2M(p|a)-M(\alpha^{*}_{a}|a)=(p-\alpha^{*}_{a})+C^{2}_{p,a}

with |Cp,a2|≤γ|C^{2}_{p,a}|\leq\gamma. The desired result then follows by repeating the argument of Lemma A.4.
